hints: Think about what type of intermolecular force acts between all three simple covalent molecules $\text{HCl}$, $\text{HBr}$ and $\text{HI}$, and what has to be overcome when they boil.
Compare the size of the electron clouds from $\text{Cl}$ to $\text{Br}$ to $\text{I}$ and link this to how strong the temporary dipoles become.
walkthrough:
See what boiling really breaks**
Picture $\text{HCl}$, $\text{HBr}$ and $\text{HI}$ as small separate molecules. When they boil you are not breaking the strong $\text{H-X}$ covalent bond inside each molecule, you are only pulling whole molecules apart from each other. So the boiling point is controlled by the weak forces between molecules.

Link electrons to strength of forces**
All three have induced dipole-dipole forces, also called London dispersion forces. Iodine is much larger than chlorine or bromine, so an $\text{HI}$ molecule has many more electrons. Its big electron cloud is easily distorted to form larger temporary dipoles, giving stronger attractions to neighbours. Stronger attractions need more heat to overcome, so $\text{HI}$ boils highest.

Final answer: $\text{HI}$ has the greatest number of electrons per molecule.
This gives stronger induced dipole-dipole (London dispersion) forces between $\text{HI}$ molecules, so more energy is needed to separate them.

hints: Recall where hydrogen bonding occurs and how its strength compares with the induced dipole forces in $\text{HCl}$, $\text{HBr}$ and $\text{HI}$.
Use that comparison to decide whether the $\text{HF}$ bar should be drawn lower than $\text{HCl}$ or higher than $\text{HI}$.
walkthrough:
Spot the special force in HF**
Fluorine is very electronegative and small, and it has a lone pair, so $\text{H-F} \cdots \text{H-F}$ can form hydrogen bonds between molecules. $\text{HCl}$, $\text{HBr}$ and $\text{HI}$ cannot form hydrogen bonds in the same way, they rely mainly on induced dipole forces.

Predict the bar position**
Hydrogen bonds are much stronger than induced dipole-dipole forces. Even though $\text{HF}$ has fewest electrons, the extra hydrogen bonding more than makes up for it. So you draw the $\text{HF}$ bar taller than the $\text{HI}$ bar, showing the highest boiling point, and explain it by the stronger total intermolecular forces.

Final answer: Draw bar for $\text{HF}$ with boiling point above $\text{HI}$ (above about 238 K).
The sum of hydrogen bonds (plus induced dipoles) in $\text{HF}$ is stronger than the sum of induced dipoles (plus permanent dipoles) in $\text{HCl}$ / $\text{HBr}$ / $\text{HI}$, so more energy is needed to separate $\text{HF}$ molecules.

hints: Start from the words formation and one mole, what is being made and how much?
Remember the two standard conditions that must be quoted for any standard enthalpy change, the starting materials and their states.
walkthrough:
Unpack the word formation**
Formation means making the compound from nothing but its elements. For $\text{HI(g)}$ that is $\frac{1}{2}\text{H}_{2} + \frac{1}{2}\text{I}_{2} \rightarrow \text{HI}$. The definition always refers to making exactly one mole of the compound.

Add the word standard**
Standard means the elements must be in their normal, most stable form at 298 K and 100 kPa, for example $\text{H}_{2}\text{(g)}$ and $\text{I}_{2}\text{(s)}$. So the full definition is the energy change when one mole is formed from its elements in their standard states.
Final answer: The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states under standard conditions.

hints: Write products over reactants using partial pressures $p$, raising each to the power of its balancing number in $\text{H}_{2}\text{(g)} + \text{I}_{2}\text{(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{HI(g)}$.
walkthrough:
Build products over reactants**
For $K_{p}$ you always put the partial pressure of the products on top and reactants below. Here the product is $\text{HI}$ and the reactants are $\text{H}_{2}$ and $\text{I}_{2}$. Because the equation has $2\text{HI}$, the top term is squared: $$K_{p} = \frac{p_{\text{HI}}^{2}}{p_{\text{H}_{2}} \times p_{\text{I}_{2}}}$$ No units are included for $K_{p}$ at this level unless stated.
Final answer: $K_{p} = \dfrac{p_{\text{HI}}^{2}}{p_{\text{H}_{2}} \times p_{\text{I}_{2}}}$

hints: Substitute $p_{\text{HI}} = 4800 \text{ Pa}$ and $p_{\text{H}_{2}} = p_{\text{I}_{2}} = 895 \text{ Pa}$ directly into your $K_{p}$ expression, remembering to square the top.
walkthrough:
Substitute and calculate**
Put the numbers straight in: $$K_{p} = \frac{(4800)^{2}}{(895)(895)}$$ $$K_{p} = \frac{23040000}{801025} = 28.76$$ This rounds to about $28.8$. Because the top has $\text{Pa}^{2}$ and the bottom has $\text{Pa}^{2}$, the units cancel.
Final answer: $K_{p} = \dfrac{4800^{2}}{895 \times 895} = 28.8$ (accept 28.76 or 29, no units)

hints: Use $\Delta H_{f}^{\ominus} = +26.5 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ to work out $\Delta H$ for $\text{H}_{2} + \text{I}_{2} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{HI}$, is the forward reaction endothermic or exothermic?
Recall how lowering temperature affects an endothermic forward reaction and what that does to the proportion of products and hence $K_{p}$.
walkthrough:
Find the sign of delta H for the reaction**
Each mole of $\text{HI}$ needs $+26.5 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ to form from its elements, so making $2$ moles needs about $+53 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. That makes the forward reaction $\text{H}_{2} + \text{I}_{2} \rightarrow 2\text{HI}$ endothermic.

Apply lower temperature**
Lowering temperature from $200^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $100^{\circ}\text{C}$ favours the exothermic direction to release heat. Here that is the backward direction. Equilibrium shifts left, $p_{\text{HI}}$ falls relative to $p_{\text{H}_{2}}$ and $p_{\text{I}_{2}}$, so the ratio $p_{\text{HI}}^{2} / (p_{\text{H}_{2}}p_{\text{I}_{2}})$ gets smaller and $K_{p}$ decreases.

Final answer: $K_{p}$ decreases.
Formation of $2\text{HI}$ is endothermic ($\Delta H = +53 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$), so lowering temperature shifts equilibrium to the left, favouring $\text{H}_{2}$ and $\text{I}_{2}$, decreasing $p_{\text{HI}}$ and $K_{p}$.

hints: Identify the products as $\text{I}_{2}$ and $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ and balance H and I atoms first, then check O atoms.
walkthrough:
Balance the atoms**
Hydrogen in $\text{HI}$ must end up in $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$, and iodine ends up in $\text{I}_{2}$. Start with $4\text{HI}$ to give $4\text{H}$ and $4\text{I}$. That makes $2\text{I}_{2}$ and $2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$, and $2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ needs one $\text{O}_{2}$. So: $$4\text{HI} + \text{O}_{2} \rightarrow 2\text{I}_{2} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$

hints: Assign oxidation numbers to I in $\text{HI}$ and $\text{I}_{2}$, has it increased or decreased?
Assign oxidation numbers to O in $\text{O}_{2}$ and $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ and decide which change is reduction.
walkthrough:
Track iodine**
In $\text{HI}$, H is $+1$ so I is $-1$. In $\text{I}_{2}$, each I is $0$. The number has gone up from $-1$ to $0$, which means electrons lost. That is oxidation.

Track oxygen**
In $\text{O}_{2}$, each O is $0$. In $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$, O is $-2$. The number has gone down from $0$ to $-2$, which means electrons gained. That is reduction. Because oxidation and reduction happen together, this is a redox reaction.

Final answer: I in $\text{HI}$ is $-1$ to $0$ in $\text{I}_{2}$, increase so oxidised / oxidation.
O in $\text{O}_{2}$ is $0$ to $-2$ in $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$, decrease so reduced / reduction. Both occur so redox.

hints: Count the total moles of gas on each side of $2\text{I}_{2}\text{(g)} + \text{N}_{2}\text{H}_{4}\text{(g)} \rightarrow 4\text{HI(g)} + \text{N}_{2}\text{(g)}$.
Recall how pressure in a fixed volume at fixed temperature depends on the total number of gas molecules.
walkthrough:
Count the gas moles**
Left side: $2 + 1 = 3$ moles of gas. Right side: $4 + 1 = 5$ moles of gas. Starting with $2$ mol $\text{I}_{2}$ plus $1$ mol $\text{N}_{2}\text{H}_{4}$ you finish with $4$ mol $\text{HI}$ plus $1$ mol $\text{N}_{2}$.

Link moles to pressure**
In a sealed container the volume and temperature are fixed, so pressure depends only on how many gas particles are hitting the walls. More moles means more collisions, so pressure goes up.

Final answer: Pressure increases.
Total gas moles increase from 3 mol reactants to 5 mol products, and at constant volume and temperature pressure is directly proportional to number of moles of gas.

hints: Place P in the centre with three I atoms around it, each single bond is one shared pair with one dot from P and one cross from I (or vice versa).
Check octets and lone pairs, P in Group 15 brings 5 outer electrons and each I in Group 17 brings 7, how many non-bonding electrons remain on each atom?
walkthrough:
Draw the three bonds**
Put P in the middle and one I at each corner. Phosphorus shares one of its electrons with one electron from each iodine to make three $\text{P-I}$ bonding pairs. Show each bond as a dot plus a cross together.

Complete the octets**
P started with 5 outer electrons, 3 are used in bonds so 2 remain as one lone pair on P. Each I started with 7, 1 is used in the bond so 6 remain as three lone pairs on each I. Every atom now has 8 electrons in its outer shell.

Final answer: P central bonded to three I by single covalent bonds (three shared pairs).
P has one lone pair, each I has three lone pairs, all outer shells complete (8 electrons around each atom).

hints: Notice $\text{PI}_{3}\text{(s)} + 3\text{H}_{2}\text{O(l)}$ splits apart using water to give two acids, what name is given to splitting by water?
walkthrough:
Recognise splitting by water**
In step 2, water breaks the $\text{P-I}$ bonds to form $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{3}$ and $\text{HI}$. Any reaction where water breaks a compound apart in this way is called hydrolysis.

hints: Recall the Bronsted-Lowry definition based on $\text{H}^{+}$ transfer, what does an acid do?
Think about what the word strong adds, how far does the dissociation go in water?
walkthrough:
Separate the two words**
Bronsted-Lowry acid simply means a proton donor, it gives away $\text{H}^{+}$ to a base. For example $\text{HI} \rightarrow \text{H}^{+} + \text{I}^{-}$.

Add the meaning of strong**
Strong means it does this completely. In water every acid molecule splits to release $\text{H}^{+}$, there is essentially full dissociation, not a reversible equilibrium.

Final answer: Proton ($\text{H}^{+}$) donor.
Fully dissociates / fully ionises in aqueous solution.

hints: Remove one $\text{H}^{+}$ from the acid $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{3}$ to leave its conjugate base, remember to adjust the charge.
walkthrough:
Remove a proton**
A conjugate base is what is left after the acid donates one $\text{H}^{+}$. Take $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{3}$ minus $\text{H}^{+}$: $$\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{3} - \text{H}^{+} \rightarrow \text{H}_{2}\text{PO}_{3}^{-}$$ The charge becomes $1-$.
Final answer: $\text{H}_{2}\text{PO}_{3}^{-}$

hints: Draw the two possible carbocations from adding $\text{H}^{+}$ to $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH=CH}_{2}$, which carbon gets the $\text{H}^{+}$ to leave the positive charge on the more substituted carbon?
Think about why a secondary carbocation is more stable than a primary one in terms of electron donation from alkyl groups.
walkthrough:
Compare the two routes**
If $\text{H}^{+}$ adds to the end $\text{CH}_{2}$, the positive charge lands on the middle carbon giving $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C}^{+}\text{HCH}_{3}$, a secondary carbocation. If $\text{H}^{+}$ adds the other way, you get a primary carbocation $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{C}^{+}\text{H}_{2}$. The secondary route wins.

Explain the extra stability**
Alkyl groups push electron density toward the positive carbon by the positive inductive effect. The secondary carbocation has two methyl groups feeding electrons to the $\text{C}^{+}$, while the primary has only one. That extra donation spreads the charge and lowers energy, so 2-iodopropane forms faster as the major product.

Final answer: Major product is 2-iodopropane.
Formed via the more stable secondary carbocation, stabilised by greater positive inductive effect from two alkyl (methyl) groups.

hints: Start the first step with the $\text{C=C}$ pi electrons attacking the $\delta^{+}$ H of $\text{H-I}$, and show the $\text{H-I}$ bond breaking onto I.
Identify the intermediate formed when H adds to the terminal carbon, where is the positive charge?
Show the lone pair on $\text{I}^{-}$ forming the new $\text{C-I}$ bond to give $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CHICH}_{3}$.
walkthrough:
Attack by the double bond**
The $\text{C=C}$ is electron rich and $\text{H}$ in $\text{H}^{\delta+}-\text{I}^{\delta-}$ is electron poor. Draw a curly arrow from the double bond to the H, to make a new $\text{C-H}$ bond on the end carbon. At the same time draw a curly arrow from the $\text{H-I}$ bond onto I, giving $\text{I}^{-}$. This leaves the positive charge on the middle carbon: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C}^{+}\text{HCH}_{3}$.

Capture of the carbocation**
Now the $\text{I}^{-}$ has full lone pairs and the carbocation is strongly electrophilic. Draw a curly arrow from a lone pair on $\text{I}^{-}$ straight to the $\text{C}^{+}$ to form the $\text{C-I}$ bond.

Show the correct product**
The H has added to the $\text{CH}_{2}$ end and I has added to the middle carbon, giving $\text{CH}_{3}-\text{CHI}-\text{CH}_{3}$, which is 2-iodopropane. Check you have shown charges, lone pair on $\text{I}^{-}$, and both curly arrows starting in the correct electron source.

Final answer: Step 1: curly arrow from $\text{C=C}$ to $\text{H}$ of $\text{H-I}$ and curly arrow from $\text{H-I}$ bond to I, forming $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C}^{+}\text{HCH}_{3}$ secondary carbocation + $\text{I}^{-}$.
Step 2: curly arrow from lone pair on $\text{I}^{-}$ to $\text{C}^{+}$.
Product $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CHICH}_{3}$ (2-iodopropane).
